Landscape Architecture Landscape architecture is a 126-credit curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Landscape Architecture (B.L.A.) degree.
Accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board of the ASLA, the curriculum is designed to prepare undergraduates for professional careers in public and private practice.
Landscape architecture is a profession that involves the design, planning, preservation, and restoration of the landscape by applying art, science, and technology to achieve the best use of our land and water resources.
Landscape architects design and plan parks, plazas, and recreation areas; residential, institutional and commercial developments; transportation facilities, new towns and campus landscapes, and green infrastructure.
They are also involved in planning and designing landscapes in coastal and inland developments impacted by climate.
The requirements of this curriculum include preparation in the basic arts and sciences.

The major includes 63-64 credits of professional core classes (LAR 101, 201, 202, 243, 244, 300, 301, 302, 343, 344, 345, 346, 353, 354, 443, 444, 445, 447, 450); 28-29 credits of supporting requirements (ART 207; GEG 101; PLS 150; CHM 100, 101 or 103 or PHY 109, or GEO 100, or 103; CPL 410, CPL 434, 538; MTH 111103; and PLS 200); and 7-8 credits of supporting electives.

Students are required to own a P.C. laptop computer by the time they enter the program.

Accreditation standards regarding staff and facilities limit the number of students accepted into the major to 20 per year.

The Department of Mathematics’ name does not accurately and fully reflect the research work, course and degree offerings, and trajectory of the department.
A more representative name for the department is the Department of Mathematics and Applied Mathematical Sciences.
Furthermore, with national trends leaning towards applied math, it is imperative that students (current and prospective) and colleagues (at URI and outside of URI) are aware of our applied math research and programs.

This name change is expected to help us in recruiting students, developing research collaborations (both within and outside the institution), and attracting new hires in applied math.
According to the U.S.
Bureau of Labor of Statistics, “Employment in math occupations is projected to grow 27 percent from 2019 to 2029, much faster than the average for all occupations, and will add about 56,100 jobs.
Growth is anticipated as businesses and government agencies continue to emphasize the use of big data, which math occupations analyze.”1 Applied mathematics is very broadly defined as using mathematics to solve problems in a wide variety of fields of study.
The name applied mathematical sciences is more focused on applying mathematics to sciences, (including a recent trend in mathematical biology, a direction in which we intend to grow) and will include the department’s involvement in the fields of actuarial science (currently done as a double major with finance) and our growing work in data science.
The department officially voted to change the department name to Department of Mathematics and Applied Mathematical Sciences on September 14, 2020. 1 https://www.bls.gov/ooh/math/home.htm

Degree Offerings.
The department has two track options at all levels, B.S. general and applied math option, M.S. pure and applied math track, and Ph.D. pure and applied math track.
The applied math tracks, at both the B.S. and Ph.D. level, have been offered for decades.
The B.S. applied math option is selected by the majority (over 67%) of B.S. math majors.
Because of this track’s popularity, in 2018 the faculty broadened the applied track offering at the M.S. level and also created the accelerated five-year B.S. – M.S. program in applied math.
Currently, more than half of our M.S. and Ph.D. graduate-level students are in the applied math track.
Additionally, the department is now in the process of creating a one-year graduate certificate in Applied Mathematics and exploring a Biomathematics minor.
With the College of Business, the department developed a curriculum outline that leads to a double major in finance and applied math (unofficially called pre-actuarial science track).
This curriculum prepares students for the first actuarial exam and provides a foundation for successful employment as an actuary.

When funding was available, the department also brought students on well-received day trips to PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) in New York.
In fact, one of our recent applied math graduates, Lauren Black, has taken a position as an associate actuary at PWC directly after graduation.
A senior manager at PwC, Larry Rubin was consulted with structuring our current curriculum.
According to the U.S.
Bureau of Labor of Statistics, “Employment of actuaries is projected to grow 18 percent from 2019 to 2029, much faster than the average for all occupations.”2 Currently there are 9 double finance and applied math majors and the department seeks to expand interest in the area of financial mathematics.
Course Offerings.
The department has always had two course codes, MTH and AMS (Applied Mathematical Sciences) and offers numerous applied math courses, e.g.
MTH 441 Introduction to Partial Differential Equations, MTH 418/518 Matrix Analysis, MTH 471/571 Numerical Analysis, MTH 472 Numerical Linear Algebra, MTH 481/581 Optimization Methods, MTH 572 Numerical Partial Differential Equations, AMS 490 Intermediate Topics in Applied Mathematics, and AMS 590 Advanced Topics in Applied Mathematics.

We also plan to propose, with the AMS course code, the following courses: AMS 210 Introduction to Mathematics Biology, AMS 310 Mathematical Modeling, AMS 410 Mathematical Biology, AMS 528 Mathematical and Computational Analysis of Data, and AMS/DSP 393G Introduction to Predictive Analytics.
Research/Activities.
In addition to having some faculty members with earned doctorates in Applied Mathematics, our faculty conduct research in applied math topics.
Areas include, but are not limited to, Numerical Linear Algebra, Mathematical Biology and Modeling, Financial Mathematics, Applied Probability, Combinatorics, Graph Theory, Partial Differential Equations, and Difference Equations.
Below is a brief summary of some of the work being done by our faculty. - Development of a statistical/linear algebra method that is used for computing the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for extremely large data sets.
Used in numerous applications (e.g. image processing, genomics, robotics).

It was featured as a chapter in the book Handbook of Big Data, a bases for svds.m in the commercial software MATLAB, and the R-package (irlba) has been downloaded over 2,500,000 times.3 2 https://www.bls.gov/ooh/math/actuaries.htm 3 https://ipub.com/dev-corner/apps/r-package-downloads/ (need to type in irlba under Packages – select cumulative) 2

Discrete random structures are essential in the design of algorithms and error correcting codes.

Nowadays, trading is performed using an electronic double auction system where offers to buy are matched with offers to sell.

Most stock exchanges in the world are operating within this new framework and while every exchange has its own rules, many follow the same principles.
An array that stores and displays the information of the price and the quantity at which people are willing to buy or sell certain asset is called a Limit Order Book.
Understanding its statistical properties has become of critical importance to many financial institutions such as banks, hedge funds and independent market participants to improve the way they perform their trades: via algorithmic trading. - Research is done in developing a systematic understanding and numerical methods in relation to polynomial and rational eigenvalue problems.
